Electrical Fundamentals
 Mutual Inductance: 5 Essential Formulas Made Easy and Clear
 When the changing flux of one coil links a second coil, a voltage appears in the second coil without any wire between them. That shared flux is the secret behind transformers, current sensors, wireless chargers and even unwanted crosstalk on a printed circuit board.
 M = k√(L1 L2) 
 Coupling Coefficient 
 Dot Convention 
 Series Aiding 
 Series Opposing 
 Two coils placed close together share part of their magnetic flux, and a change of current in one induces a voltage in the other. Mutual inductance measures how strong that link is, and five simple formulas cover almost every practical calculation.
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn mutual inductance, the coupling coefficient, the dot convention and how coupled coils behave in series aiding and series opposing connections.
 What Is Mutual Inductance?
 Mutual inductance is the property of two coils by which a changing current in one coil induces a voltage in the other coil through their shared magnetic flux. It is the two coil partner of self inductance, which is explained in inductor working principle .
 The induced voltage follows Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction , and its direction follows Lenz's law. The symbol is M and the unit is the henry, the same unit used for self inductance L.
 Image credit: Circuit Digest . Diagram courtesy of Circuit Digest, shown here for educational reference. 
 The dots in the figure mark the ends of the two windings that have the same polarity at any instant. You will see these dots on transformer symbols and datasheets, and they decide whether the mutual term is added or subtracted.

 How Shared Flux Creates a Voltage
 When current i1 flows in coil 1, it produces a magnetic field. Part of that flux, called the mutual flux, also passes through the turns of coil 2, while the rest, called leakage flux, closes its path without reaching coil 2.
 If i1 changes, the mutual flux changes and a voltage appears across coil 2 even with no electrical connection. The process works in both directions, and for linear materials M12 equals M21, so one value M describes the pair.
 Formula 1: v2 = M × di1 ÷ dt 
 Formula 1b: M = N2 × Φ21 ÷ i1 
Example: M = 3 mH, current in coil 1 rises by 2 A in 1 ms
di1 ÷ dt = 2 ÷ 0.001 = 2000 A per second
 v2 = 0.003 × 2000 = 6 V 
 Because only a changing current induces voltage, steady DC through coil 1 gives no output from coil 2. This is why a transformer does not work on pure DC, a point covered in transformer turns ratio and secondary voltage .
 Do You Know?
 Michael Faraday showed mutual induction in 1831 with two coils wound on one iron ring. The galvanometer on the second coil kicked only when he closed or opened the switch on the first coil, never while current flowed steadily.
 5 Essential Mutual Inductance Formulas
 No. Formula Use 
 1 v2 = M × di1 ÷ dt Induced voltage in coil 2 
 2 M = k × √(L1 × L2) M from self inductances and coupling 
 3 L aiding = L1 + L2 + 2M Series, fluxes add 
 4 L opposing = L1 + L2 minus 2M Series, fluxes oppose 
 5 M = (L aiding minus L opposing) ÷ 4 Measuring M on the bench 
 These five relations solve most textbook and field problems on coupled coils. The lecture notes from the University of Ruse also give the stored energy as W = ½ L1 i1² + ½ L2 i2² ± M i1 i2, where the sign depends on whether the fluxes aid or oppose.
 Coupling Coefficient k Explained
 In mutual inductance work, the coupling coefficient k tells what fraction of the flux of one coil links the other. It ranges from 0, with no shared flux, to 1, where every line of flux links both coils.
 Formula 2: M = k × √(L1 × L2) 
 k = M ÷ √(L1 × L2), with 0 ≤ k ≤ 1 
Example: L1 = 4 mH, L2 = 9 mH, k = 0.5
√(4 × 9) = √36 = 6 mH
 M = 0.5 × 6 = 3 mH 
 Mutual inductance can never exceed the geometric mean of the two self inductances, which is why k cannot be greater than 1. Coils on a closed iron or ferrite core have k close to 1, while air core coils spaced apart may have k well below 0.5.
 Tightly Coupled
 Common closed core, windings interleaved, k close to 1.
 Best for: power and signal transformers
 k near 1 
 Loosely Coupled
 Air gap or distance between coils, k roughly 0.05 to 0.5.
 Best for: wireless charging and RFID
 Flexible 
 Uncoupled
 Coils far apart or at right angles, k near 0.
 Best for: separate inductors on a PCB
 Isolated 
 Wireless phone chargers and RFID tags work with loose coupling, so they use resonance to transfer energy efficiently. On a PCB, by contrast, designers try to keep k near zero between neighbouring traces, as shown in PCB crosstalk reduction .
 Quick Tip
 To reduce unwanted mutual inductance between two inductors on a board, place them at right angles and keep them apart. Shielded inductors also confine their flux and cut coupling sharply.
 Dot Convention and the Sign of Mutual Inductance
 The dot rule says that a current entering the dotted end of one coil induces a voltage that is positive at the dotted end of the other coil. In other words, the dotted ends rise and fall together.
 1
 Mark Currents
 Draw the assumed current direction in each coil.
 2
 Check Dots
 See whether each current enters or leaves the dotted end.
 3
 Same Side
 If both enter or both leave dots, the mutual voltage term is positive.
 4
 Opposite Side
 If one enters and one leaves a dot, the mutual voltage term is negative.
 5
 Write KVL
 Add the mutual term M di ÷ dt in each loop equation with that sign.
 With these signs in place, each coil loop is solved with ordinary Kirchhoff’s voltage law . In AC analysis the mutual term becomes j ω M times the other current, a reactance just like those in impedance and reactance in AC circuits .
 Do You Know?
 Transformer makers mark polarity with dots, with H1 and X1 labels, or with letters such as 1U and 2U. Reversing one winding by mistake when paralleling two transformers can cause a large circulating current.
 Mutual Inductance in Series Aiding and Opposing Coils
 When two coupled coils are connected in series so that current enters both dotted ends, their fluxes add and the total inductance rises. This is called series aiding, and Circuit Digest gives L = L1 + L2 + 2M for it.
 If one coil is reversed, current enters one dot and leaves the other, the fluxes oppose and the total becomes L = L1 + L2 minus 2M. Circuit Digest notes that k can reach a maximum of 1, which means 100 percent coupling.
 Formula 3: L aiding = L1 + L2 + 2M 
 Formula 4: L opposing = L1 + L2 minus 2M 
Example: L1 = 4 mH, L2 = 9 mH, M = 3 mH
L aiding = 4 + 9 + 6 = 19 mH
 L opposing = 4 + 9 minus 6 = 7 mH 
 For coupled coils in parallel the result is L = (L1 L2 minus M²) ÷ (L1 + L2 minus 2M) when aiding and L = (L1 L2 minus M²) ÷ (L1 + L2 + 2M) when opposing. Compare these with the simple rules in series vs parallel circuits , which hold only when M is zero.

 Second Example: Measuring M With an LCR Meter
 You rarely know k in advance, but you can find mutual inductance with an LCR meter. Connect the two coils in series and measure L, then reverse one coil and measure again, which gives L aiding and L opposing.
 Formula 5: M = (L aiding minus L opposing) ÷ 4 
Example: L aiding = 30 mH, L opposing = 14 mH
M = (30 minus 14) ÷ 4 = 4 mH
L1 + L2 = (30 + 14) ÷ 2 = 22 mH, so L1 = L2 = 11 mH if identical
 k = 4 ÷ √(11 × 11) = 0.364 
 The larger of the two readings is always the aiding connection, which also tells you where the dots are. This simple bench method is handy for checking transformer polarity and coil samples before a design is frozen.
 Measure L1 and L2 Each coil alone, other coil open
 Series Reading 1 Coils in series, note L
 Reverse One Coil Swap its two leads
 Series Reading 2 Note the new L
 Calculate Larger is aiding, M = difference ÷ 4, then k
 Quick Tip
 Measure at a frequency close to the real operating frequency, because ferrite permeability and winding capacitance change the reading. Keep the meter leads short and twisted.
 Where Mutual Inductance Is Used
 Power Transformers
 Step voltage up or down with k close to 1.
 Current Transformers
 Measure large currents with isolated secondaries.
 LVDT Sensors
 Displacement changes coupling between coils.
 Wireless Charging
 Loosely coupled coils transfer power through air.
 Common Mode Chokes
 Coupled windings block noise current.
 Flyback Converters
 Coupled inductor stores and transfers energy.
 In a current transformer , the primary conductor and secondary winding share flux on a toroidal core. In an LVDT , a moving core changes the coupling to two secondaries, so the output voltage tracks position.
 A common mode choke uses two tightly coupled windings so that noise currents in the same direction see high inductance while the differential signal passes. A flyback converter uses a coupled inductor whose leakage, set by imperfect k, causes the voltage spike that the snubber must absorb.
 Myth: Mutual inductance always needs an iron core.
 Fact: Air core coils also have mutual inductance, only with a lower coupling coefficient.
 Myth: k can exceed 1 with a very good core.
 Fact: k is at most 1 by definition, since M cannot exceed the square root of L1 times L2.
 Myth: Coupled coils pass DC from one to the other.
 Fact: Only a changing current induces voltage, so steady DC is not transferred.
 Myth: Reversing a winding does not matter.
 Fact: Reversal changes the sign of M and can halve or double the total inductance.
 Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
 Confirm the dot or polarity marks before connecting windings.
 Use the correct sign of M in every KVL equation.
 Check that k is between 0 and 1 in all calculations.
 Measure inductance at the real operating frequency.
 Allow for leakage inductance in converter and transformer designs.
 Keep sensitive coils at right angles to noisy inductors.
 A frequent design error is ignoring leakage, which is the part of each self inductance not shared with the other coil. In galvanic isolation transformers, higher isolation spacing usually lowers k and raises leakage, so the trade off must be checked.
 Advantages of Mutual Inductance Coupling
 Transfers energy with no electrical contact.
 Provides galvanic isolation between circuits.
 Allows voltage and current scaling by turns ratio.
 Enables non contact sensing of position and current.
 Limitations
 Works only with changing current, not steady DC.
 Leakage flux causes losses and voltage spikes.
 Unwanted coupling creates crosstalk and noise.
 Core saturation limits the useful current range.

 Mutual Inductance FAQ
 What is mutual inductance in simple words?
 It is the ability of one coil to induce a voltage in a nearby coil when its current changes. The two coils share part of their magnetic flux.
 The unit is the henry, the same as self inductance. A value of 1 henry means a change of 1 ampere per second in one coil induces 1 volt in the other.
 What is the coupling coefficient k?
 It is the fraction of flux from one coil that links the other coil. Its value lies between 0 for no coupling and 1 for perfect coupling.
 It is calculated as k = M ÷ √(L1 × L2). Power transformers have k very close to 1, while air core coils spaced apart have much lower values.
 What does the dot convention tell us?
 The dots mark winding ends that have the same instantaneous polarity. A current entering a dot induces a positive voltage at the dot of the other coil.
 This rule fixes the sign of the mutual inductance term in every circuit equation you write. Getting it wrong changes the predicted voltages and the total inductance of series coils.
 What is the difference between series aiding and series opposing?
 In series aiding, current enters both dotted ends and the fluxes add, so the total is L1 plus L2 plus twice the mutual inductance. In series opposing, one coil is reversed and the total becomes L1 plus L2 minus twice that value.
 The difference between the two totals is four times the mutual term. Measuring both with an LCR meter is the easiest way to find the mutual inductance of real coils.
 Does mutual inductance work with DC?
 Only a changing current produces a changing flux, so steady DC induces no voltage in the second coil. A short pulse appears only when the DC supply is switched on or off.
 This is why transformers need AC or switched DC to operate, as mutual inductance acts only on change. Current transformers also give no output on a steady DC primary current.
 Why is mutual inductance important in PCB design?
 Neighbouring traces and loops share flux, so a fast current change in one induces noise in another. This unwanted mutual inductance is a major cause of crosstalk on circuit boards.
 Designers reduce it by shrinking loop areas, adding solid ground planes and spacing fast traces apart.
